They're both kind of asking about the major - how do I make them different? Also, I don't know if my game work is worthy of a portfolio."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "These essays have different focuses even though they're both about DMD. The first one is about WHY digital media design. Focus on: Why creativity and interdisciplinary work matter to you, why you need both art and technology, the process of being a creator. Think about it philosophically - maybe how having multiple identities prepares you for interdisciplinary work.

The second essay is HOW you'll pursue this at Penn specifically. This is where you mention: specific DMD classes you want to take, research opportunities in computer graphics or VR, clubs and organizations at Penn. This one is tactical - show you've researched the program.

For the portfolio - your games are absolutely valuable! DMD is perfect for game developers. Even if it's 'recommended' not 'required,' you should submit. Include Synthoria for sure - it demonstrates both technical skills and creative vision. If you have any Blender work, animations, or graphics, include those too. They're looking for potential, not perfection.

Also, reach out to the program director Adam Mally. Keep the email brief: 'I'm a prospective DMD applicant and aspiring game developer from California. I would appreciate the opportunity to speak with you and learn more about the program. Do you have availability for a brief conversation next week?' The meeting is really an excuse to pitch yourself - talk about Synthoria and gauge if DMD is the right fit versus straight CS."} ], "metadata": { "intelligence_type": "program_specific_strategy", "week": "086", "quality_score": 9 } }, { "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "Help a student make their essay details more specific and personal rather than generic."}, {"role": "user", "content": "I wrote 'In my poster-clad bedroom, my fingers hover over the WASD keys.' How do I make it more personal?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "The issue is that WASD keys are universal to all gamers - they don't tell us anything unique about YOU. Every gamer uses WASD, but not every gamer has your specific setup. Let's replace generic gaming details with personal ones.

Instead of just 'poster-clad bedroom,' what posters do you actually have? What color is your keyboard, headset, or mouse? Is your room bathed in RGB lighting or soft monitor glow? Do you have a specific chair, a certain desk setup?

For example: 'In my poster-clad bedroom, bathed in the soft glow of monitors, my fingers dance across a pink and white keyboard as I adjust my headset.' Now we see YOUR space, not just any gamer's space.

The pink and white keyboard tells us something - maybe you're feminine in a masculine-dominated space, maybe you like to personalize your tools, maybe you refuse to conform to the all-black 'serious gamer' aesthetic. These specific details do narrative work that generic details can't.

Also consider sensory details unique to your experience: Is your mom making biryani downstairs while you game? Can you hear your sister practicing violin?
